name: Globe and Mail cryptic crossword No 3,243

clue.text: Cuisine that’s surprisingly warm

indicators.note: something that turns out surprisingly has come out in an unexpected form, so the letters land in an unexpected order

blocks.note: all twelve letters taken as written, apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: A food critic remarks that a style of cooking turned out to be unexpectedly hot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Warm' looks like a temperature of food, but it is the definition in its sense of eager and keen; the twelve letters of the first two words rearrange to ENTHUSIASTIC.
explanation.definitionFit: A warm welcome or warm support is hearty and eager, which is a close synonym for being keenly enthusiastic.

clue.text: Suggestion upset 7 too

indicators.note: to upset something is to knock it over and throw it into disorder, so the letters are scrambled

blocks.note: the answer to 7-across
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone protests that a hint has upset them as well.
explanation.walkthrough: The cross-reference 7 means the solution to 7-across, NEVER, and 'too' joins it as part of the fodder rather than meaning 'also'.
explanation.definitionFit: An overtone is an implied secondary meaning or hint carried along with the plain words, which is a kind of suggestion.

clue.text: Scottish island without one large plant

indicators.note: 'without' means lacking, so the following item must be taken away from the word before it

blocks.note: Tiree is an island in the Inner Hebrides off western Scotland
one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: A Scottish island described as having no single big plant growing on it, plausible for windswept Hebridean land.
explanation.walkthrough: Tiree is famously flat and nearly treeless, which makes the surface neatly apt. Removing the I from TIREE leaves TREE.
explanation.definitionFit: A tree is the standard example of a large woody plant with a trunk and branches, so the description fits as a broad definition.

clue.text: Sportsperson covering for fish?

blocks.note: first meaning: a player who bats in cricket or baseball
second meaning: the flour-and-egg coating fried around fish

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests someone who protects or covers for fish; the question mark flags that the second half is a playful definition of the coating in fish and chips.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both the player wielding a bat in baseball or cricket and the liquid mixture used to coat fried food.

clue.text: In favour of axes, at first we always recommend indirect fighting

indicators.note: 'at first' points to what comes at the start, so only the opening letter of each word is kept

blocks.note: pro means for or in favour of
the x and y axes of a graph
the opening letters of these three words

explanation.surface: A strategist, keen on axes, advises always using roundabout methods of combat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Axes' looks like chopping tools, but it is the two graph axes, X and Y. The definition sits at the end of the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A proxy war is a conflict where major powers fight through third parties instead of directly, so the combat is indirect.

clue.text: Shakespeare was associated with this rising star

indicators.note: in a down clue, rising means reading from bottom to top, which turns the word around

blocks.note: a nova is a star that suddenly brightens

explanation.surface: Shakespeare is linked with a young celebrity on the way up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rising star' reads as one phrase meaning an up-and-coming talent, but it splits into a reversal signal and a word for a star.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare was born in Stratford-upon-Avon and is called the Bard or Swan of Avon, after the river through his hometown.

clue.text: No one verifies internally

indicators.note: 'internally' means on the inside, so the letters sit within the run of words

blocks.note: the letters run across the inside of these two words

explanation.surface: A complaint that nobody checks things in-house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No one' reads as a single phrase meaning nobody, but only 'No' is the definition; 'one' starts the hidden run.
explanation.definitionFit: As an emphatic refusal, saying never carries the same meaning as an outright no, so the two words can swap.

clue.text: Rare to remove coat before competitor’s appearance

indicators.note: a coat is the outer layer, so taking it off leaves only the inner letters

blocks.note: the inner two letters once the outer ones are stripped
a rival is a competitor; the 's stands for is, joining to the definition

explanation.surface: It is unusual for a contestant to show up without taking off their coat first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Before' places one piece ahead of the other. The possessive on 'competitor’s' acts as 'is', linking to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An arrival is the act of coming on the scene, which is what making an appearance means, as in a guest's entrance.

clue.text: Twisting or bending old collapsible spanner?

indicators.note: twisting something wrenches it out of shape, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: twelve letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A worn-out folding wrench that twists or bends when you use it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old' looks like part of the definition but belongs to the fodder. 'Spanner' looks like a wrench but means something that spans a river; the nursery rhyme says London Bridge is falling down, hence collapsible.
explanation.definitionFit: A bridge spans a river, and the London Bridge of the rhyme famously keeps falling down, so a playful description fits it.

clue.text: Gathering the VAR’s broken

indicators.note: something broken is smashed apart, so its letters can be put back together differently

blocks.note: the letters as written, apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: A football crowd gathers to grumble that the video referee system is not working.
explanation.walkthrough: VAR is the video assistant referee used in football; its letters, with THE and S, rearrange into a word for the crop-gathering season.
explanation.definitionFit: A harvest is the gathering in of ripe crops, and the word also names the collected yield itself.

clue.text: Element 10, next to nothing brought back

indicators.note: bringing something back returns it the way it came, so the word reads backwards

blocks.note: X is the Roman numeral for ten
none means nothing at all

explanation.surface: A chemistry note: element number ten, sitting beside an empty space, has been returned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Element 10' looks like neon, atomic number 10, but the number is the Roman numeral and 'Element' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Xenon is a chemical element, one of the noble gases, atomic number 54, used in flash lamps and headlights.

clue.text: Playing words with care — this gives one point for each

definitions.text: this gives one point for each

indicators.note: playing with something means toying with it and moving it around, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A word-game player is careful, with each tile scoring one point.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a word game like Scrabble scoring tiles; in fact it is football, where a draw earns each side one league point. A score draw is a draw with goals, such as 1-1.
explanation.definitionFit: In football leagues a drawn match earns each team one point, so a draw with goals scored is a result giving both sides a point.

clue.text: This makes room for soldiers to encourage limiting ops in retreat

indicators.note: an army in retreat goes back the way it came, so the word runs backwards
to limit something is to set bounds around it, so one piece is enclosed by the other

blocks.note: to egg on is to urge or encourage
taken as written, military operations

explanation.surface: A military order: clear space for the troops by urging operations to pull back.
explanation.walkthrough: Soldiers are strips of toast dipped into a soft-boiled egg in Britain; the spoon scoops out the top so they fit, which makes the military surface a disguise.
explanation.definitionFit: An egg spoon digs out the top of a boiled egg, creating space into which toast strips, nicknamed soldiers, can be dipped.

clue.text: Prime time with Oscar

blocks.note: T is the abbreviation for time
W is a standard abbreviation for with
Oscar is the NATO alphabet word for O

explanation.surface: Peak viewing hours shared with an Academy Award.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prime time' looks like a single phrase about television scheduling, but 'Prime' alone is the definition, a noun meaning a prime number.
explanation.definitionFit: Two is the smallest prime number and the only even one, so as a noun it is a prime.

clue.text: Best opportunities to buy broadcast equipment for boats

indicators.note: to broadcast something is to send it out over the air to be heard, so what matters is the sound

blocks.note: the best bargains are top sales

explanation.surface: An advert promises the best bargains on air for nautical gear.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads like a shopping channel selling boat gear, but the first phrase is spoken: TOP SALES sounds like the sails above a ship's lowest ones.
explanation.definitionFit: Topsails are the sails set above the lowest sail on a mast, part of the rigging that sailing vessels carry.

clue.text: Amazing card

blocks.note: first meaning: excellent, superb, as slang
second meaning: the single-pip playing card

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as praise for a person who is a card, a joker, but the two words are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is informal praise meaning excellent and also the name of the playing card ranked highest or lowest in a suit.

clue.text: Gossip about mushy sprout in eating establishment

indicators.note: something mushy is soft and pulped out of shape, so the letters lose their order
'about' means around, so one piece is wrapped around another

blocks.note: gab is idle chatter
taken as written

explanation.surface: Diners gossip about an overcooked Brussels sprout served at a restaurant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mushy' looks like a description of badly cooked vegetables but signals the letter shuffle; GAB is split around the result.
explanation.definitionFit: A gastropub is a pub that serves high-quality restaurant-style food, so it is a place people go to eat.

clue.text: Easy chance to score with model

blocks.note: first meaning: in football, an open goal that should not be missed
second meaning: a person who poses for a painter or photographer

explanation.walkthrough: The surface hints at romance with a model; in fact both halves define one word. In British sport slang an easy chance is a sitter.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a gift of a scoring opportunity in sport and someone who sits while an artist paints a portrait.

clue.text: President’s cap

blocks.note: first meaning: the surname of a recent US president
second meaning: to outdo or top something

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as a hat belonging to a president, famously a red cap, but the apostrophe-s is a link meaning 'is' between two meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: The surname of the American president is also a verb meaning to beat or outdo, just as to cap a story is to top it.

clue.text: Unpleasant fruit mostly ending in jelly

indicators.note: 'mostly' means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped
the ending of a word is its final letter, so only that one is kept

blocks.note: the ugli is a Jamaican citrus fruit, here without its last letter
the closing letter of this word

explanation.surface: A fruit dessert that ends up mostly as an unappetising jelly.
explanation.walkthrough: The ugli fruit is a knobbly grapefruit-tangerine cross whose name is a play on ugly, so the parse comes close to spelling the answer itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Ugly describes something disagreeable or nasty, as in an ugly mood or scene, so it fits unpleasant as an adjective.

clue.text: Drums beat — I’m panicking to a certain extent

indicators.note: 'to a certain extent' means partly, so only part of the run of words is used

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of the first word, the whole second word, and the start of the third

explanation.surface: A drummer hammers away, partly in a panic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beat' looks like it goes with the drums, but it supplies the opening letter of the hidden run.
explanation.definitionFit: Timpani are kettledrums, the large tuned copper drums played in an orchestra's percussion section.

clue.text: Wizard of 1000 years

blocks.note: M is the Roman numeral for a thousand
an age is a long period of years

explanation.surface: A sorcerer who has lived a thousand years.
explanation.walkthrough: '1000 years' looks like a millennium, a phrase describing the wizard, but it splits into a Roman numeral and a word for a long span of time.
explanation.definitionFit: A mage is a magician or sorcerer, a somewhat literary or fantasy-game term for one who practises magic.

clue.text: Dish from California area

blocks.note: Cal is a standard abbreviation for California
a zone is an area

explanation.surface: A regional speciality from part of California.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests Californian cuisine, but the food is Italian; the state supplies only its short form.
explanation.definitionFit: A calzone is a folded, stuffed Italian pizza turnover, a food served as a dish in restaurants.

clue.text: Convict following gut, mostly in prison camp

indicators.note: 'mostly' means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped
'following' means coming after, so the piece it describes is placed second rather than first

blocks.note: the word without its last letter
a lag is British slang for a convict, as in old lag

explanation.surface: A prisoner trusts their instinct, most of the time, while held in a labour camp.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Following' places the convict after the shortened gut. Lag is British slang for a prisoner, usually a habitual one.
explanation.definitionFit: The Gulag was the Soviet system of forced labour camps, and the word now names any such harsh prison camp.
